content: 1. Approximately 0.17% of the population treated with cold knife conization (CKC) will experience premature delivery. 2. No data was identified regarding the risk of infertility following treatment for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher (CIN 2+). 3. It was assumed that the risk of major infections in true negatives (TN) and false negatives (FN) would be zero, as these groups were not treated. However, 0.088% of individuals treated with CKC are expected to develop major infections. 4. Similarly, the risk of minor infections in TN and FN was assumed to be zero due to the absence of treatment. In contrast, 0.09368% of individuals treated with CKC are expected to develop minor infections. 5. The number of cancers detected during first-time screening was calculated based on data from Sankaranarayanan et al. (2005). For single screening tests, the number of cancers detected was defined as screen-detected cancers in women participating in the screening program. For tests involving colposcopy, the number was calculated as the sum of screen-detected and clinically detected cancers. 6. In cases where multiple tests were used (e.g., HPV testing followed by visual inspection with acetic acid [VIA]), the test that detected the greater number of cancers was considered. No cancers were assumed to be detected in the no screen group. 7. The cancer detection numbers presented do not represent the annual incidence of cervical cancer but rather the prevalence of cancer at the time of screening. 8. For the no screen group, calculations were based on the same assumptions as for FN, except for premature delivery, which was considered a baseline risk in the population. 9. It was assumed that the recurrence of CIN is constant across age groups. However, the incidence of cervical cancer and associated mortality increases with age, reducing the overall recurrence of CIN (as a proportion of those with CIN will progress to cancer or die). 10. These data are intended primarily for comparing different screen-and-treat strategies rather than for comparisons within columns for different age groups. 11. The expert panel recommends a strategy of screening with an HPV test followed by VIA and treatment with cryotherapy (or loop electrosurgical excision procedure [LEEP] if cryotherapy is not suitable) over a strategy of screening with an HPV test followed by colposcopy (with or without biopsy) and treatment with cryotherapy (or LEEP if not suitable). This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 12. While reductions in cancer and related mortality may be slightly greater with HPV testing followed by colposcopy compared to HPV testing followed by VIA, the panel agreed that the benefits of either strategy outweigh the harms and costs. However, the cost differences between the strategies remain uncertain. 13. Colposcopy may have greater resource implications due to increased provider training, quality control, waiting times, and the potential for more women to be lost to follow-up. 14. It is unclear whether women would perceive a difference between VIA and colposcopy, though biopsies during colposcopy may be less acceptable than VIA. 15. This recommendation applies to women regardless of their HIV status. 16. The quality of evidence for diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) and comparisons between strategies is low. There is also low-to-very-low-quality evidence for treatment effects and the natural progression of CIN, often with inconsistent results across studies. 17. The benefits of HPV testing followed by colposcopy (e.g., reduction in CIN recurrence, cervical cancer, and related mortality) may be greater than with HPV testing followed by VIA. However, there may be greater overtreatment with HPV testing followed by colposcopy without biopsy. 18. There is little to no difference in the number of cancers detected between the two strategies. 19. High value was placed on a screen-and-treat strategy compared to no screening, as qualitative studies have shown that women find screening tests and immediate treatment acceptable once they decide to be screened. 20. High value was also placed on minimizing overtreatment and potential complications, as well as on the acceptability of biopsies compared to visual inspection. 21. Adding colposcopy to HPV testing may have greater resource implications than adding VIA due to increased training, quality control, waiting times, and the potential for more women to be lost to follow-up. 22. The evidence for HPV testing followed by VIA compared to HPV testing followed by colposcopy for detecting CIN 2+ is based on low-quality data. 23. The outcomes of screen-and-treat strategies include mortality from cervical cancer, cervical cancer detection rates, CIN 2+ detection rates, major bleeding, premature delivery, infertility, sexually transmitted infection (STI) detection, major infections, and minor infections. 24. The overall quality of evidence for these outcomes is very low, primarily due to very low-quality evidence for treatment effects and natural progression/history data. 25. Mortality from cervical cancer was assumed to be zero in TN and FP groups. Calculations for cervical cancer mortality assumed 250 deaths per 350 women with cervical cancer. 26. Cervical cancer incidence was assumed to be zero in TN and FP groups. The incidence rate was based on an age-standardized rate of 350 cervical cancers per 1,000,000 women in Eastern Africa, with 2% having CIN 2+ and a subsequent 30% regression rate, leaving 14,000 women with persistent CIN 2+. 27. CIN 2+ was assumed to be absent in TN and FP groups. Calculations in the model were based on a 70% natural persistence rate of CIN 2+ without treatment (30% regression) in FN cases. The incidence of cervical cancer and mortality was subtracted from the CIN 2+ in FN cases.
